source_excerpts.text:
The strongest extension is an operational readout theorem, not a faster Gibbs-learning algorithm.
I obtained a self-contained finite-dimensional proof of the following statement:
For bounded-locality, bounded-incidence Hamiltonian parameter directions, one fixed randomized single-qubit measurement loses at most an extensive amount of Fisher information relative to optimal quantum readout—even with calibrated, independent detector errors.
The consequence is sharper than a conditioning statement: when equilibrium parameter sensitivity is superextensive, this fixed local measurement preserves its leading information. Moreover, a measured scalar variance can certify that near-optimality without evaluating a partition function.
This result does not assume the earlier global covariance candidate. Its complete derivation is below and in the manuscript. Independent proof review and original priority remain unestablished.
astra_local_readout_information.pdf · astra_local_readout_research_packet.zip
I examined the predecessor’s decisive ordering:
\[ \langle \mathcal G_iP_a,\mathcal G_jP_c\rangle_K = \langle P_a,\mathcal G_i\mathcal G_jP_c\rangle_K, \]
followed by local approximation.
I did not find a decisive defect in moving the exact thermal adjoint before truncation, or in the corresponding support-counting argument. That does not independently validate the complete Gaussian locality, frequency-tail, and uniform-constant construction. The repository appropriately still records N711 as an unreviewed candidate with an open independent-reconstruction gate. 
The important limitation is that its auxiliary operator need not generate a completely positive evolution. Thus its coercivity does not automatically provide a physical Gibbs sampler, rapid equilibration, or inexpensive optimization.

\[ \boxed{\text{measured covariance}-\text{thermal response covariance}.} \]
Neither covariance needs to have decaying correlations or bounded largest eigenvalue. Their difference can nevertheless be bounded uniformly. That is the cancellation mechanism used here.

For disjoint supports, the product measurement reproduces the quantum second moment, including any long-range correlation. It adds no cross-covariance error.
For overlapping supports, direct evaluation gives
\[ |N_{ac}| \le \left(\frac3{\eta^2}\right)^k-1. \]
Each candidate overlaps at most \(1+k(\Delta-1)\) candidates, counting itself. Hence
\[ 0\preceq N\preceq\nu_{\mathrm{meas}}I, \]
where
\[ \nu_{\mathrm{meas}} = [1+k(\Delta-1)] \left[\left(\frac3{\eta^2}\right)^k-1\right]. \tag{6} \]
This step applies to arbitrary states. It does not assume Gibbs structure or independent quantum outcomes.
For any Hermitian \(A\), the Brooks–Harris inequality gives
\[ 0\le \operatorname{Var}_\rho(A) -\operatorname{Cov}^{\mathrm{BKM}}_\rho(A,A) \le \frac{\beta}{12} \operatorname{Tr}\rho[A,[H,A]]. \tag{7} \]
This is an established thermal correlation inequality. The variance-minus-susceptibility quantity is also an established object, often called quantum variance. Neither is being claimed as new. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.2882)
For completeness, its spectral proof uses the logarithmic and arithmetic means of two Gibbs probabilities:
\[ L_{ij}=\frac{p_i-p_j}{\log p_i-\log p_j}, \qquad T_{ij}=\frac{p_i+p_j}{2}. \]

The double-commutator weight is \(4x^2L_{ij}/\beta\), giving (7).

Suppose a family of systems and parameter directions satisfies
\[ \frac{u_n^TF_Qu_n}{\|u_n\|_2^2}\longrightarrow\infty, \]
while \(\beta,g,k,\ell,\Delta,\eta\) remain fixed.
Equation (3) immediately yields
\[ \boxed{ \frac{u_n^TF_{\mathrm{loc}}u_n}      {u_n^TF_Qu_n} \longrightarrow1. } \tag{13} \]
For example, if a collective direction has \(\|u_n\|^2=\Theta(n)\) and quantum Fisher information \(\Theta(n^{1+\alpha})\), \(\alpha>0\), the relative information loss is \(O(n^{-\alpha})\).
Thus, when superextensive equilibrium sensitivity exists, an entangling readout is unnecessary to preserve its leading information.
This does not assert that every model exhibits enhanced scaling. It also does not convert equilibrium sensitivity into a free metrological advantage: preparing equilibrium states, especially across competing phases, remains a separate resource.
For a scalar perturbation
\[ H(t)=H_0+tA_u, \]
let
\[ f=u\cdot Y,\qquad v=\operatorname{Var}(f),\qquad C_u=u^TCu,\qquad q=\|u\|_2^2. \]
Then
\[ C_u\le v\le C_u+\nu q, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb Ef=-\beta C_u. \tag{14} \]
The information obtainable from the first moment through local error propagation is
\[ F_{\mathrm{mom}}=\frac{\beta^2C_u^2}{v}. \]
It satisfies
\[ F_{\mathrm{mom}} \le u^TF_{\mathrm{loc}}u \le u^TF_Qu \le\beta^2C_u, \]
and therefore
\[ \boxed{ \frac{F_{\mathrm{mom}}}{u^TF_Qu} \ge \frac{C_u}{C_u+\nu q}. } \tag{15} \]
This is not merely an existence statement about a complicated likelihood statistic. When the response is enhanced, the ordinary sample mean of one explicitly computable feature is nearly optimal.
At a calibrated reference point \(t_0\), the locally unbiased estimator
\[ \widehat t = t_0+ \frac{\overline f-\mathbb E_{t_0}f}{-\beta C_u(t_0)} \]
has exact variance
\[ \operatorname{Var}_{t_0}(\widehat t) = \frac{v}{N\beta^2C_u^2}. \]
Calibration acquisition and finite-displacement bias control are not included in that formula.
Equation (14) implies
\[ (v-\nu q)_+\le C_u\le v. \]
Therefore a directly measured scalar variance gives
\[ \boxed{ \beta^2\frac{(v-\nu q)_+^2}{v} \le u^TF_{\mathrm{loc}}u \le u^TF_Qu \le \beta^2v. } \tag{16} \]
The lower expression is defined as zero when \(v=0\).
